sentences.text: Last week, sitting right at its own break -even, Strategy bought 1,036 BTC per its latest filing.

before.text: But that's not quite how it works, so let's focus on the details here.
For one thing, according to Strategies count, funds tracking those indexes hold about 30 million of its shares, which is roughly 3 % of the company.
But the key distinction here is that those funds would be selling Strategies stock, not Bitcoin.
A removal wouldn't force strategy to sell any of its BTC stack.
Sailor's view is that the capital MSCI controls is, quote, day minimis.
He's hardly a neutral party, of course, but on strategy's figures, it isn't a lot of stock.
So MSCI could knock strategy's share price around, but it can't push Bitcoin through its 200 -day moving average on its own.
However, we then have to ask, if no forced seller is coming for Bitcoin, why is that 200 -day still in danger, and who's actually left buying?
Well, the one big buyer that hasn't blinked is the company that we've just been talking about.

after.text: And how it paid for them is significant, because those coins were bought with money raised by Strategy selling more of its own shares.
So, its buying only keeps going for as long as investors keep wanting Strategy's stock.
which is the stock MSCI could knock around later this month.
And indeed, Bitcoin wasn't even the biggest thing that it spent money on.
Strategy bought about $82 million of Bitcoin last week, but more than twice that was spent on its own preferred shares.
So, Strategy is looking vulnerable right now.
BTC's price is closing in on the company's average purchase price, its financing needs aren't going away, and an MSCI exclusion could make raising fresh money even harder.
Meanwhile, Bitcoin ETFs are bleeding billions and the broader market is still reeling from the midterm sell -off.
And yet, with all of those complex issues ongoing, it comes back to something simple on the chart, Bitcoin's 200 -day moving average.
